metadata.title: zERC20 Privacy Token Protocol - Audit Map Batch 1

attack_vectors_applied.finding: LiquidityManager._wrap() at line 249-277 validates amount != 0 and receiver != address(0). For native tokens, msg.value == amount is enforced. For ERC20, SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom is used. The 248-bit constraint is enforced in zERC20._update() at line 153-159 via `if (value > type(uint248).max) revert ValueTooLarge()`.
Wrap is atomic within a single transaction. nonReentrant modifier applied. No partial state exists between transferFrom and mint.
No unbounded loops. Gas cost is predictable. No amplification vector found.
SafeERC20 reverts on transfer failure. Custom errors ZeroAmount, ZeroReceiver properly bubble up.
ReentrancyGuardTransient prevents reentrancy. No cross-function race conditions identified.

counterexample.scenario: Attacker attempts to wrap with amount = type(uint256).max to cause overflow in reward calculation
preconditions: Attacker has underlying token balance
LiquidityManager has sufficient approval
attack_steps: 3. ERC20 balance check fails in transferFrom
counterexample.expected_outcome: Transaction reverts due to insufficient balance. Even if balance existed, IncentiveLib._rawWrapReward has overflow protection via maxK check.
counterexample.guard_found: ERC20 balance check + SafeERC20 + IncentiveLib maxK validation

guards_identified.description: ZeroAmount and ZeroReceiver checks at function entry
msg.value validation for native and ERC20 variants

audit_results.notes: Wrap boundary is well-protected. The 248-bit constraint is enforced at the zERC20 level for all token operations. Recommend running forge fuzz tests to validate edge cases around type(uint248).max values.

attack_vectors_applied.finding: No explicit state machine pattern. Wrap is atomic - validates, transfers, calculates reward, mints in sequence.
Atomic execution within nonReentrant. No intermediate pausable states that could leave wrap incomplete.
No state machine to corrupt. Single atomic operation.
Reverts atomically on any failure - no cleanup needed.
ReentrancyGuardTransient prevents re-entry during wrap execution.

counterexample.scenario: Attacker attempts to leave wrap in partial state by causing revert after transferFrom but before mint
preconditions: Attacker controls malicious ERC20 with callback in transferFrom
attack_steps: 1. Deploy malicious ERC20 that reverts in callback after balance update
counterexample.expected_outcome: Entire transaction reverts atomically. No partial state. Note: LiquidityManager uses immutable UNDERLYING_TOKEN set at construction, so malicious token attack is not possible without compromised deployment.

guards_identified.description: UNDERLYING_TOKEN is immutable - set at construction

audit_results.notes: No explicit state machine but wrap is atomic. The design choice to use immutable token references prevents token substitution attacks. Recommend fuzz testing for state consistency.

attack_vectors_applied.finding: LiquidityManager._unwrap() validates amount != 0 and receiver != address(0) at lines 281-282. zERC20.burn is called which checks balance via ERC20._burn.
Burn occurs BEFORE underlying transfer. If transfer fails, tokens already burned - potential issue. However, SafeERC20.safeTransfer reverts on failure causing atomic revert.
InsufficientLiquidity check prevents unwrap when pool is drained. No unbounded loops.
Custom errors InsufficientLiquidity, UnderlyingSendFailed. SafeERC20 handles transfer errors.
nonReentrant applied. Fee calculation uses storage state that cannot be manipulated mid-execution.

counterexample.scenario: Attacker attempts to unwrap more zERC20 than they hold
preconditions: Attacker has some zERC20 balance
counterexample.expected_outcome: Transaction reverts with ERC20InsufficientBalance error from OpenZeppelin ERC20._burn

audit_results.notes: Unwrap boundary is well-protected. The burn-before-transfer pattern is safe due to atomic transaction semantics. Fee calculation uses ceiling division per IncentiveLib to protect protocol.

attack_vectors_applied.finding: IncentiveLib.quoteUnwrapFee uses validated FeeParams. validateFeeParams enforces targetLiquidity <= MAX_TARGET_LIQUIDITY and k <= K_BPS_DENOM.
Fee calculation is pure function - no state transition concerns.
O(1) computation. No loops or recursion.
_rawUnwrapFee returns 0 on edge cases (T=0, L=0, amount=0). Safe defaults.
Pure function with no storage access in core computation.

counterexample.scenario: Attacker attempts to get zero fee by manipulating rounding
preconditions: Small unwrap amount
Specific liquidity/target ratio
attack_steps: 1. Calculate amount where floor(fee) = 0 but ceil(fee) > 0
counterexample.expected_outcome: _ceilDiv at line 281-286 ensures (a % b != 0) ? q + 1 : q, so fee is always rounded UP. Protocol is protected from fee undercollection.

audit_results.notes: Fee calculation correctly uses ceiling division. The library is mathematically sound for fee protection. Recommend fuzz testing with edge case values.

attack_vectors_applied.finding: zERC20._update() at line 153-154 enforces: `if (value > type(uint248).max) revert ValueTooLarge()`. This applies to ALL token operations including transfer, mint, burn.
_update is called via super._update which is ERC20._update. Balance updates and hash chain updates occur atomically.
O(1) hash computation per transfer. No amplification.
ValueTooLarge custom error. Clear revert path.
ERC20 standard semantics. No reentrancy in _update.

counterexample.scenario: Attacker attempts to transfer value > 2^248-1 to break ZK circuit compatibility
preconditions: Attacker somehow has balance > 2^248-1 (impossible under normal conditions)
counterexample.expected_outcome: Transaction reverts with ValueTooLarge() at line 154. ZK circuit compatibility preserved.

guards_identified.description: if (value > type(uint248).max) revert ValueTooLarge() - BN254 field constraint

audit_results.notes: CRITICAL: The 248-bit constraint is enforced correctly in _update which is called for ALL token movements. This is essential for ZK circuit soundness. The check is on the transfer value, not balance - which is correct as individual transfers must fit in circuit.

attack_vectors_applied.finding: Hash chain update at line 157 uses ShaHashChainLib.compute(). Need to verify SHA-256 with 248-bit truncation matches ZK circuit.
Hash chain is updated atomically with balance update in _update. Index is incremented after hash chain update.
Single SHA-256 computation per transfer. O(1).
No error conditions in hash computation - pure mathematical operation.
Hash chain update is atomic with transfer. No race window.

counterexample.scenario: Mismatch between on-chain hash computation and ZK circuit hash computation
preconditions: Different implementations of SHA-256 truncation
attack_steps: 2. Attempt to prove using ZK circuit
counterexample.expected_outcome: If implementations match, proofs succeed. If they don't match, proofs fail and protocol is unusable (availability issue, not security issue).
counterexample.guard_found: Requires verification that ShaHashChainLib matches ZK circuit implementation

guards_identified.description: emit IndexedTransfer($.index++, from, to, value) - deterministic ordering

audit_results.notes: Hash chain mechanism appears correct but requires verification against ZK circuit implementation in zkp/ directory. The emit after hash update ensures events match state.

attack_vectors_applied.finding: Verifier.teleport() at line 306-328 validates proof BEFORE any state modification. IWithdrawDecider.verifyOpaqueNovaProof called at line 325. singleTeleport uses IWithdrawVerifier.verifyProof at line 347.
Proof verification -> root validation -> recipient validation -> monotonicity check -> mint. Correct order.
Groth16 verification is O(1) with fixed proof size. No amplification vector.
InvalidProof error on failed verification. Clear revert.
totalTeleported monotonicity prevents replay. No reentrancy concern as mint is last operation.

counterexample.scenario: Attacker submits invalid Groth16 proof to mint tokens
preconditions: Attacker has malformed proof data
attack_steps: 1. Construct invalid proof with tampered public inputs
counterexample.expected_outcome: Transaction reverts with InvalidProof() error at line 325 or 347. No tokens minted.
counterexample.guard_found: Groth16/Nova proof verification before state modification

audit_results.notes: CRITICAL BOUNDARY: ZKP verification is correctly placed before any state modification. The soundness of the protocol depends on the correctness of the verifier contract implementations (IRootDecider, IWithdrawDecider, IWithdrawVerifier).

attack_vectors_applied.finding: Monotonicity check at line 377: `require(value > currentTotal, NothingToWithdraw(currentTotal, value))`. Strict inequality (>) prevents replay.
totalTeleported[recipient] updated at line 379 AFTER mint calculation at line 378. This is correct order.
Single storage read/write. O(1).
NothingToWithdraw error clearly indicates replay attempt.
Within single transaction. No race window.

counterexample.scenario: Attacker attempts double-spend by replaying same proof
preconditions: Valid proof that was already used
attack_steps: 1. Submit valid teleport proof (succeeds, totalTeleported updated)
counterexample.expected_outcome: Second call reverts with NothingToWithdraw(currentTotal, value) because value > currentTotal check fails.

guards_identified.description: require(value > currentTotal, NothingToWithdraw(currentTotal, value)) - strict inequality

audit_results.notes: CRITICAL: The strict inequality (>) is essential. Using >= would allow double-spend. The current implementation correctly uses > which ensures totalTeleported only ever increases. No setter function exists for totalTeleported - it's only modified in _teleport.

attack_vectors_applied.finding: Root validation at lines 366-368 checks expectedRoot != 0 and expectedRoot == transferRoot. Both local (provedTransferRoots) and global (globalTransferRoots) roots are validated.
Root validation occurs before recipient validation and before mint. Correct order.
Single mapping lookup. O(1).
ExpectedRootZero and TransferRootMismatch errors clearly identify failure mode.
Root is read from storage within transaction. No race window.

counterexample.scenario: Attacker attempts to teleport using non-existent root reference
preconditions: Attacker has valid proof format but referencing invalid root
attack_steps: 1. Construct proof referencing rootHint that was never proved
counterexample.expected_outcome: Transaction reverts with ExpectedRootZero(rootHint) at line 367.

audit_results.notes: Root validation is comprehensive - checks both existence (!=0) and equality. The isGlobal flag correctly selects between local and global root arrays.

attack_vectors_applied.finding: Hub._lzReceive() at lines 312-331 validates origin.srcEid via eidToPosition mapping check. If eidToPosition[origin.srcEid] == 0, reverts with TokenNotRegistered.
Validation occurs before any state modification. Payload decoding happens after EID check.
Single mapping lookup. Payload length validated at line 320.
TokenNotRegistered and InvalidPayloadLength errors.
LayerZero guarantees ordered delivery. No race conditions.

counterexample.scenario: Attacker sends spoofed LayerZero message from unregistered chain
preconditions: Attacker controls node on unregistered chain
attack_steps: 1. Send LayerZero message with unregistered srcEid
counterexample.expected_outcome: Transaction reverts with TokenNotRegistered(origin.srcEid) at line 318.
counterexample.guard_found: eidToPosition mapping check + LayerZero setPeer configuration

audit_results.notes: CRITICAL BOUNDARY: Hub correctly validates source EID before processing. Combined with LayerZero's setPeer mechanism, this provides defense-in-depth. Only registered verifiers can send root updates.

attack_vectors_applied.finding: Token index derived from eidToPosition at line 323: `uint256 index = pos - 1`. pos is validated to be > 0 before this point.
Root is only updated if transferTreeIndex > currentTreeIndex (line 325). Monotonic update prevents stale data.
Array access with bounded index. MAX_LEAVES = 64.
Silent skip of stale updates (line 325-327). Could consider logging for debugging.
Monotonic index prevents out-of-order issues.

counterexample.scenario: Root collision between different tokens
preconditions: Two different EIDs map to same index
attack_steps: 1. Register token A with EID_A -> position 5
2. Register token B with EID_B -> position 5 (collision)
counterexample.expected_outcome: Not possible - registerToken at line 159 checks if EID already registered and increments array position. Each EID gets unique index.

guards_identified.description: Sequential push to arrays with eidToPosition = index + 1

audit_results.notes: Root storage is correctly indexed by token position derived from EID. The monotonic index check prevents replay of stale roots. 1-based eidToPosition with 0 meaning unregistered is a common pattern.

attack_vectors_applied.finding: Verifier._lzReceive() at line 440 explicitly checks: `require(origin.srcEid == $.hubEid, InvalidHubSource(origin.srcEid))`. Defense-in-depth with setPeer.
Validation before storage update. Global root only stored at line 444 after validation.
Single mapping write. O(1).
InvalidHubSource error clearly identifies unauthorized source.
Duplicate root handling at line 443 - only writes if slot is empty (==0).

counterexample.scenario: Attacker sends fake global root from non-Hub source
preconditions: Attacker controls LayerZero message from different EID
attack_steps: 1. Send message with arbitrary global root from EID != hubEid
counterexample.expected_outcome: Transaction reverts with InvalidHubSource(origin.srcEid) at line 440.

audit_results.notes: DEFENSE-IN-DEPTH: Verifier has explicit EID validation in addition to LayerZero's setPeer mechanism. This is good practice even if setPeer already validates the source.

attack_vectors_applied.finding: Global root storage at lines 443-446. Payload decoded as (globalRoot, aggSeq_). No validation of root value itself - relies on Hub integrity.
Write-once semantics: only writes if slot is empty (line 443). Cannot overwrite existing roots.
Single mapping write. latestAggSeq tracking at lines 448-450.
No explicit error on duplicate - silent skip. Event emitted on new storage (line 445).
Write-once pattern prevents race to overwrite.

counterexample.scenario: Attacker attempts to overwrite existing global root
preconditions: Valid global root already stored for aggSeq
attack_steps: 1. Hub broadcasts root for aggSeq N (stored)
2. Attacker somehow sends different root for same aggSeq N
counterexample.expected_outcome: Condition is false, new root is NOT stored. Original root preserved.

audit_results.notes: Write-once semantics ensure global roots cannot be overwritten once set. This is critical for preventing root manipulation after initial storage.

attack_vectors_applied.finding: relayTransferRoot at lines 392-414 sends to $.hubEid (immutable). Payload encoded as (root, index) at line 403. Only sends if root != 0 (line 401).
latestRelayedIndex updated at line 413 AFTER successful _lzSend. If send fails, index not updated.
Single _lzSend call. Gas fee quoted and validated at lines 404-406.
NoProvedRoot and InsufficientMsgValue errors. Clear failure modes.
Anyone can call relayTransferRoot. Multiple calls relay same root (idempotent at Hub due to index check).

counterexample.scenario: Attacker manipulates destination EID to send root to wrong Hub
preconditions: Attacker has control over hubEid value
counterexample.expected_outcome: hubEid is set only during initialize() and has no setter. Cannot be changed after deployment.

guards_identified.description: if (root == 0) revert NoProvedRoot() - prevents relaying empty root
Fee validation: if (msg.value < quotedFee.nativeFee) revert InsufficientMsgValue
hubEid set only in __Verifier_init, no setter function

audit_results.notes: Outbound message encoding appears correct. hubEid immutability ensures messages always go to intended Hub. Payload format (root, index) must match Hub's expected TRANSFER_PAYLOAD_LENGTH of 64 bytes.

attack_vectors_applied.finding: broadcast at lines 192-214 takes targetEids as parameter. Each EID validated via eidToPosition check in _quoteBroadcast at line 299.
aggSeq incremented at line 202 BEFORE send loop. If any send fails, aggSeq already incremented - potential inconsistency.
Loop over targetEids. If many EIDs, gas could exceed block limit. MAX_LEAVES = 64 provides upper bound.
NativeFeeMismatch and FeeRefundFailed errors. _lzSend may revert on failure.
No reentrancy guard but _lzSend is trusted call to LayerZero endpoint.

counterexample.scenario: Partial broadcast - some verifiers receive root, others don't
preconditions: Broadcast with multiple targetEids, insufficient gas for all
attack_steps: 3. _lzSend fails for EID_C due to gas/other issue
counterexample.expected_outcome: Entire transaction reverts if any _lzSend fails (EVM atomic semantics). aggSeq increment is safe because it happens in same transaction.

guards_identified.description: if (msg.value < totalNativeFee) revert NativeFeeMismatch - pre-send fee validation

audit_results.notes: Broadcast iterates over targetEids array. The caller provides which EIDs to broadcast to - there's no automatic broadcast to ALL registered tokens. This is by design but means caller must specify complete list. MAX_LEAVES=64 bounds worst case.

attack_vectors_applied.finding: PoseidonAggregationLib.computeAggregationRoot at line 265/283. Uses pre-computed zeroHash array for sparse tree. MAX_LEAVES = 64 (height-6 tree).
Aggregation is view-only computation. State update (aggSeq) happens separately.
Tree computation is O(n log n) where n <= 64. Bounded.
Library functions are pure/view. No explicit error handling needed.
Pure computation from snapshot of transfer roots.

counterexample.scenario: Aggregation root mismatch between on-chain and ZK circuit
preconditions: Different Poseidon implementations
attack_steps: 3. Roots differ due to implementation mismatch
counterexample.expected_outcome: If Poseidon implementations match, roots match. If they differ, withdrawal proofs would fail to verify (availability issue, not security breach).
counterexample.guard_found: Requires verification that PoseidonAggregationLib matches ZK circuit

audit_results.notes: PoseidonT3 aggregation requires verification against ZK circuit implementation. The height-6 tree (64 leaves) matches specification. Zero-hash handling for sparse tree needs validation.

attack_vectors_applied.finding: Adaptor._innerBridgeUnderlyingToken at lines 493-523. SendParam constructed with minAmountLD = request.minAmountOut at line 501. User-provided slippage protection.
Balances debited before Stargate call at lines 484-485. If Stargate fails, tokens lost? No - revert on Stargate failure.
Single Stargate.sendToken call. Gas bounded by Stargate.
OutputTooLow error at line 481 if amountToBridge < request.minAmountOut.
nonReentrant applied to entry points. Self-call pattern for internal ops.

counterexample.scenario: MEV sandwich attack during Stargate bridge
preconditions: User sets minAmountOut too low or zero
attack_steps: 2. MEV bot front-runs Stargate pool manipulation
3. User receives much less than expected
counterexample.expected_outcome: If minAmountOut is properly set by user, Stargate enforces it. If user sets 0, they accept any slippage. UI should enforce reasonable defaults.

audit_results.notes: Slippage protection is passed through to Stargate. The user is responsible for setting appropriate minAmountOut. Zero minAmountOut is technically allowed but should be discouraged by UI. Consider adding minimum slippage floor.

attack_vectors_applied.finding: lzCompose at lines 217-249 validates: msg.sender == LZ_ENDPOINT (line 224) and _from == address(ZERC20_TOKEN) (line 225). Both are CRITICAL.
Balances credited at lines 232-233. Decode errors emit event and return (NOT revert) at lines 239-241 to prevent asset lock.
Message size bounded by LayerZero. O(1) decode.
CRITICAL: try-catch with emit DecodeBridgeRequestFailed at line 240 - does NOT revert to prevent asset lock.
nonReentrant applied. Self-call pattern for internal operations.

counterexample.scenario: Attacker calls lzCompose directly without being LayerZero endpoint
preconditions: Attacker has EOA or contract
counterexample.expected_outcome: Transaction reverts with InvalidComposeSender() at line 224.

guards_identified.description: try-catch on decodeBridgeRequest with emit DecodeBridgeRequestFailed - NO REVERT

audit_results.notes: CRITICAL: The lzCompose implementation correctly uses try-catch to prevent reverts on decode errors. This is essential to prevent assets from being stuck if malformed compose messages are received.

attack_vectors_applied.finding: decodeBridgeRequest at lines 339-341 uses OFTComposeMsgCodec.composeMsg to extract inner message, then abi.decode. External pure function allows try-catch.
Decode is pure function. No state changes.
Bounded by message size from LayerZero.
CRITICAL: If decode fails, try-catch in lzCompose catches it and emits event instead of reverting.
Pure function, no concurrency concerns.

counterexample.scenario: Malformed compose message locks assets
preconditions: User sends OFT with malformed composeMsg
attack_steps: 1. User sends zERC20 OFT with invalid BridgeRequest encoding in composeMsg
2. lzCompose receives message, attempts to decode
3. decodeBridgeRequest reverts due to invalid encoding
counterexample.expected_outcome: try-catch at line 237 catches the revert, emits DecodeBridgeRequestFailed event, returns without reverting. User's zERC20 balance is credited and can be withdrawn.
counterexample.guard_found: try-catch pattern with emit and return (not revert)

guards_identified.description: try this.decodeBridgeRequest(_message) ... catch (bytes memory revertData) { emit DecodeBridgeRequestFailed; return; }

audit_results.notes: CRITICAL: The try-catch pattern on decodeBridgeRequest is essential for asset safety. If this reverted on malformed messages, user assets would be stuck. The current implementation correctly handles this by emitting event and returning.

attack_vectors_applied.finding: zERC20.mint at lines 185-188 and burn at lines 193-196 both check: `if (msg.sender != minter()) revert OnlyMinter()`. Minter is set via setMinter (onlyOwner).
mint/burn directly call _mint/_burn after auth check. No intermediate states.
Standard ERC20 mint/burn. O(1).
OnlyMinter custom error clearly identifies authorization failure.
minter() is storage read. Owner could change minter between check and mint - but owner is trusted.

counterexample.scenario: Unauthorized contract attempts to mint zERC20
preconditions: Attacker has deployed contract that calls zERC20.mint
counterexample.expected_outcome: Transaction reverts with OnlyMinter() at line 186.

guards_identified.description: if (msg.sender != minter()) revert OnlyMinter() - in mint()
if (msg.sender != minter()) revert OnlyMinter() - in burn()
setMinter is onlyOwner - only owner can change minter

audit_results.notes: Minter authorization is correctly implemented. Only the configured minter (LiquidityManager) can call mint/burn. Owner can change minter but owner is trusted per trust model.

high_priority_recommendations: Verify ShaHashChainLib implementation matches ZK circuit SHA-256 truncation (CL-PROP-EDGE-014-USER-INITIATES-TRANSFER-02)
Verify PoseidonAggregationLib matches ZK circuit Poseidon implementation (CL-PROP-EDGE-026-HUB-TO-LAYERZERO-02)
Run fuzz tests for IncentiveLib edge cases around MAX_TARGET_LIQUIDITY bounds
Verify Groth16 verifier contract implementations (IRootDecider, IWithdrawDecider, IWithdrawVerifier) are correctly deployed
